turns.question: Which supplements have good scientific evidence of benefit for generally healthy men around age 40?
turns.objective: Explain what the evidence shows: which supplements have good scientific evidence of benefit for generally healthy men around age 40
turns.config: searchBudget=6 spendLimit=500¢ stages=[GATHER, FILL_GAPS] outputTokens=8000 wordingCheck=true
turns.shown:
Supplements with good evidence for healthy men around 40 — Not established: no source supported what this rests on.
Among the supplements I checked, only creatine has good evidence of a measurable benefit in healthy adults (the cited evidence is more tentative than this). Most other common supplements have no demonstrated benefit or insufficient evidence. This is a summary of the evidence, not advice on what suits any one person (the cited evidence is more tentative than this). Creatine, combined with resistance training. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials found that creatine plus resistance training increased lean body mass by about 1.1 kg in adults (the cited sources do not show: 1.1 kg; the cited evidence is more tentative than this). Only indicated, not established: This held across young, middle-aged and older adults. Only indicated, not established: Men gained more than women. The outcome measured is lean mass, not long-term health outcomes (the cited evidence is more tentative than this). I did not find or assess evidence on creatine's long-term safety in this search (the cited evidence is more tentative than this). [9] [10] Multivitamins and single or paired nutrients, for preventing heart disease and cancer. The US Preventive Services Task Force says the evidence is insufficient to judge benefits and harms of multivitamins. Only indicated, not established: It says the same for single or paired nutrient supplements other than beta carotene and vitamin E. The evidence review behind this found little or no benefit for cancer, cardiovascular disease and death. Only indicated, not established: The one exception was a small benefit for cancer incidence with multivitamin use. "Insufficient evidence" means the question is unresolved, not that these supplements are proven useless (the cited sources do not show: “proven”; the cited evidence is more tentative than this). [1] [2] [3] Only indicated, not established: Beta carotene and vitamin E. The Task Force recommends against both for preventing cardiovascular disease or cancer, a Grade D recommendation. Only indicated, not established: Beta carotene was linked to a higher risk of lung cancer in people at high risk of lung cancer. The Task Force's guidance applies to community-dwelling, nonpregnant adults (the cited evidence is more tentative than this). Only indicated, not established: It does not apply to people with a known nutritional deficiency. [1] [2] [3] Only indicated, not established: Vitamin D (2000 IU a day). In VITAL, a large randomized trial, vitamin D did not lower the risk of invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events compared with placebo. Only indicated, not established: VITAL enrolled men aged 50 and over and women aged 55 and over, so it does not directly cover men around 40. [4] [5] [6] Only indicated, not established: Omega-3 fish oil. In VITAL, omega-3s did not reduce the main combined cardiovascular outcome. Only indicated, not established: The trial investigators reported a 28% lower risk of heart attack as a separate finding. Only indicated, not established: A summary of the trial's results calls that finding hypothesis-generating and says it deserves further study. Only indicated, not established: It also noted that the benefit appeared mainly in people with low fish intake. Only indicated, not established: This was also in an older population than men around 40. [7] [8] [4] [5] [6] Not established: Overall. Of the supplements I looked at, only creatine combined with resistance training has meta-analytic support for a measurable benefit in healthy adults, including middle-aged adults. This conclusion is limited to what I searched. I did not find or assess other supplements, such as magnesium, protein, probiotics, or correcting a documented deficiency (the cited evidence is more tentative than this). [29]
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: The USPSTF recommends against beta carotene and vitamin E for preventing cardiovascular disease or cancer. It finds the evidence insufficient for multivitamins and for single or paired nutrients. It excludes people with a known nutritional deficiency.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: A systematic review found little or no benefit of vitamin and mineral supplements for preventing cancer, cardiovascular disease and death. The exception was a small benefit for cancer incidence with multivitamins. Beta carotene raised lung cancer risk in people at high risk.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: In VITAL, vitamin D did not lower the risk of invasive cancer or cardiovascular events. The participants were older than men around 40.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: In VITAL, omega-3s did not reduce the main combined cardiovascular outcome. Lower heart attack risk was a separate finding that needs further study. It was concentrated in people with low fish intake.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: A meta-analysis of randomized trials found creatine plus resistance training added about 1.1 kg of lean mass regardless of age group. Men gained more than women, and creatine without exercise did not help.
Caveat: Not established: Among the supplements checked, only creatine combined with resistance training has meta-analytic support for a measurable benefit in healthy adults, including middle-aged adults. The others had null or insufficient evidence.

What I couldn't establish
- Other supplements (multivitamin effects on cognition, magnesium, protein, probiotics, vitamin B12 or D for people with deficiency) — not searched, so no conclusion.
- Long-term safety of creatine in healthy men — not assessed in the sources I retrieved.
- Creatine effects specific to men aged about 40 — the evidence found covers broader age groups, not that age alone.
- c6, that only creatine plus resistance training has meta-analytic support among the supplements checked. — I searched for umbrella reviews of supplements in healthy adults. No source states this exclusive conclusion for healthy men around 40. The umbrella reviews found low-certainty cardiovascular signals for omega-3 and folate in broader adult populations. They also found moderate-to-high-certainty effe
- Folate, and other supplements not examined in this investigation — I did not check these against healthy men around 40. The umbrella review's folate signal comes from adults in general. Its authors note it may not apply to the US, where food is fortified with folate.
